answer.sourceLine: This exact English wording comes from Plutarch’s Moralia essay The Education of Children (De liberis educandis), §14, in the translation by A. R. Shilleto for Bohn’s Classical Library (1898). The thought is genuinely in the Plutarchan corpus, but two honest caveats apply: the standard modern Loeb (Babbitt, 1927) renders the same Greek as “timely silence is a wise thing, and better than any speech,” and most scholars regard this particular essay as spurious ‘pseudo-Plutarch.’

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Moralia — The Education of Children (De liberis educandis), §14
A. R. Shilleto, Bohn’s Classical Library (George Bell & Sons), 1898

source.excerpt: For silence at the proper season is wisdom, and better than any speech. And that is, I think, the reason why the ancients instituted the mysteries, that we, learning therein to be silent, might transfer our secrecy to the gods to human affairs. And no one ever yet repented of his silence, while multitudes have repented of their speaking.
trail: The exact popular wording is confirmed word-for-word in A. R. Shilleto’s 1898 Bohn translation of Plutarch’s Moralia, essay “On Education,” §14.
The standard modern Loeb translation (Babbitt, 1927) renders the same Greek differently: “timely silence is a wise thing, and better than any speech.”
The Loeb introduction notes it is “generally believed that the essay which stands first in the collected works of Plutarch cannot have been written by him” — hence ‘pseudo-Plutarch.’
source.excerptNote: As rendered by A. R. Shilleto (Bohn, 1898). The Loeb Classical Library edition (F. C. Babbitt, 1927) translates the same sentence as “For timely silence is a wise thing, and better than any speech.”
source.rightsNote: The displayed wording is A. R. Shilleto’s translation, first issued in Bohn’s Classical Library well before 1931 (the copy consulted is the 1898 George Bell & Sons printing), so the translation is in the public domain in the United States. The underlying ancient Greek text is likewise public domain.

author.heading: About Plutarch
author.metaLine: c. 46 – after 119 AD · Greek biographer, essayist & Delphic priest
author.bio: Plutarch of Chaeronea was a Greek Middle Platonist philosopher, biographer, and essayist, best known for his Parallel Lives and the sprawling collection of essays known as the Moralia. He served for decades as a priest at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi and wrote extensively on ethics, education, and self-command. The essay quoted here, The Education of Children, has circulated under his name since antiquity but is judged by most modern scholars to be the work of an imitator in his tradition — ‘pseudo-Plutarch.’

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Plutarch is broadly right — the sentence is a real passage from the Moralia — but two things quote sites never mention are worth knowing.

items.why: The precise viral phrasing — “Silence at the proper season is wisdom, and better than any speech” — is Shilleto’s specific English rendering, not Plutarch’s own words. Sites such as Goodreads print it with no source or translator at all.

The authoritative modern edition translates the same sentence as “For timely silence is a wise thing, and better than any speech” — so the popular one-liner is one of several valid renderings, not a fixed quotation.

The source essay, De liberis educandis, opens the Moralia under Plutarch’s name but is widely regarded as not genuinely his on stylistic and linguistic grounds — likely composed by a follower in his circle.

misattribution.truthLine: Real Plutarchan-corpus passage, correctly themed — but the famous wording is Shilleto’s 1898 translation of an essay most scholars think Plutarch did not actually write.

context.heading: Why the line lands
lead: The sentence sits in a section of The Education of Children on teaching boys to govern the tongue. The author argues that mastering speech — and knowing when not to use it — is no “slight and insignificant matter,” and grounds the claim in the religious mysteries, where initiates learned silence as a sacred discipline.

Its afterlife as a standalone aphorism owes everything to Victorian translation: Shilleto’s crisp “silence at the proper season is wisdom” is quotable in a way the more literal Loeb rendering is not, which is why it, and not the Greek or the Loeb, is what circulates today.
